prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength realise time measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a rare case where a clean atomic-physics idea, trapping atoms at a wavelength where the light shift cancels between the clock states, was turned into a measurement of unprecedented precision. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme and demonstrated it with strontium; Ye's group at JILA took it to the 10^-18 regime and used the clocks to measure the gravitational redshift across millimetres, to study many-body effects in the lattice, and to bound variations of constants. Several independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) have reproduced and surpassed the early results, and clock-to-clock comparisons agree. This is what I look for: a discovery-level method that tells us something new about how atoms and time behave, with a two-name credit list that is compact and has little ambiguity.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the committee may regard optical clocks as a continuation of the 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, the frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, trapped-ion control), so it may not read as a new conceptual discovery but as refinement of a measurement. Ion-clock groups and other lattice-clock pioneers (Lemonde, Takamoto and others) could also claim a share, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so practical consequences are still to come. I also have to say that this is my own field, and I may overvalue the elegance of the physics.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B034 first as a measurement advance that opens new observables (millimetre redshift, varying constants, dark-matter probes, geodesy) and notes that other groups could be argued but the decisive concept and flagship performance belong to Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I agree, and I would put the emphasis a little differently. The new observables matter, but what convinces me is that the magic-wavelength condition rests on atomic polarizabilities that can be calculated and checked, and the independent clocks agree. I accept your caution on Lemonde and Takamoto; Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy still seem to me the two clear pillars, and I would not want the prize to be widened beyond three people just to be inclusive.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B034 only fifth and warns that Hall and Haensch (frequency comb) and Wineland (ion clocks) were already recognised, so some overlap with earlier prizes may be argued.
responses.response: This is the most serious objection to my first choice and I take it seriously, but I disagree with its weight. The comb is the gearbox that makes optical frequencies countable, and ion control gave single-particle clocks. Neither contains the idea of interrogating many neutral atoms in a lattice at a magic wavelength with no Doppler or recoil shifts, which is what moved the stability and accuracy by orders of magnitude. The 2005 citation was explicitly about the comb. I think the earlier prizes strengthen the case by showing the committee considers precision metrology as physics, but I accept that the citation should be written so the novelty of the lattice is explicit.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B046) first and B034 second, emphasising that Jarillo-Herrero's 2018 experiment was decisive and that Andrei's earlier STM work is part of the record.
responses.response: I respect that case and ranked B046 fifth mainly because I defer to colleagues in condensed matter, so please correct me if I undervalue it. My reservation is maturity, not merit: the correlated phases are reproduced but the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and the credit question (Andrei, Cao, Bistritzer) is harder than for the clock. I would keep B046 as a strong candidate for a later year, but I do not think it is more ready than B034 now.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B028) first as a genuinely new class of quantum matter with robust ties between calculation and measured spectra, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a defensible trio.
responses.response: I agree that the idea is deep and that prediction followed by confirmation is exactly the pattern I like. My difficulty is with the attribution: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are missing, and Hasan has a real claim for the 3D case, so a three-person prize would have to leave out someone important. If the condensed-matter members can agree on a defensible trio, I would be willing to move B028 up, and I list it as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat optical lattice clocks as a new achievement or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether a two-name prize for Katori and Ye does justice to other lattice-clock and ion-clock pioneers, which I cannot fully resolve from the supplied credits.
How condensed-matter colleagues weigh topological insulators and twisted bilayer graphene against each other, where I rely on their judgement.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with attosecond groups at Lund and ETH, and I work in the same atomic, molecular and optical community as the clock and ultracold-atom candidates. No specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited names on the shortlist is apparent from my profile, but I flag the AMO-community closeness, especially for B011 and B034, for the chair to consider.
